extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (readers of Locke's Essay on Human Understanding)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the epistemological and psychological criteria and distinctions John Locke sets out for the mind's faculties (perception, retention/memory, discernment, composition, abstraction, etc.). Useful for philosophy students or anyone studying Locke's theory of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is the first step and degree towards knowledge and the inlet of all the materials of it; it distinguishes animals from vegetables and varies in degree across creatures and with condition (age, bodily constitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance: "Perception then being the FIRST step and degree towards knowledge, and the inlet of all the materials of it..."; Locke explains that perception may exist in some degree in all animals, but with varying quickness and number of senses. He uses this faculty to explain differences between species (e.g., oysters vs. men), notes decay of perception in old age, and emphasizes that fewer/duller senses and faculties place a creature farther from human knowledge. (See sections: 'Perception puts the difference between Animals and Vegetables', 'Perception in all animals', 'According to their condition', 'Decay of perception in old age', 'Perception the Inlet of all materials of Knowledge'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention / Memory (twofold: contemplation and revival)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention or memory is the faculty that keeps ideas received from sensation or reflection either actually in view (contemplation) or revives them after they have disappeared (memory); memory is the storehouse that allows ideas to be brought back with the additional perception that they 'have been before'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's formulation: retention is done two ways—'CONTEMPLATION' (keeping ideas actually in view) and 'MEMORY' (reviving ideas after imprinting). The memory is described as a repository: ideas are not literally present but can be revived, sometimes more or less vividly. He stresses the necessity of memory for progressing beyond present objects; without it the other faculties are largely useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing ideas: attention, repetition, pleasure and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention and repetition strengthen memory; ideas accompanied by pleasure or pain make the deepest and most lasting impressions and are therefore most easily fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: 'Attention and repetition help much to the fixing any ideas in the memory. But those which naturally at first make the deepest and most lasting impressions, are those which are accompanied with pleasure or pain.' Locke explains this as a wise ordering of nature: painful impressions supply the place of reflection in children and act faster than deliberation in adults, thereby fixing cautionary ideas in memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgetting / Causes of oblivion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas may fade and be lost if not repeated; some impressions made only once or lightly can vanish entirely, and bodily constitution or disease can accelerate decay of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's observations: examples include early sensory impressions lost in those who later lose sight, the gradual decay of images unless renewed, and how fever or disease can 'calcine' mental images. He notes that even deep impressions require renewal to persist indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory defects: oblivion and slowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal defects in memory are complete loss of ideas (oblivion) and slowness in retrieving stored ideas; extreme slowness amounts to stupidity because ideas preserved but not readily available are of little use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'First, That it loses the idea quite... Secondly, That it moves slowly...' He links ready availability of ideas to invention, fancy, and quickness of parts, and contrasts a dull man who cannot retrieve ideas in time with one who is ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment / Distinguishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Discernment—perceiving ideas as distinct from one another—is necessary for knowledge; without clear and determinate ideas the mind would have little ability to form accurate judgments or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'Another faculty ... is that of DISCERNING and DISTINGUISHING between the several ideas it has.' He stresses that clarity and determinate ideas prevent confusion even when senses vary, and that the faculty of distinguishing underpins evidence and certainty of propositions often thought innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit versus Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit consists in rapid assemblage and clever juxtaposition of ideas to create pleasant imaginings; judgment consists in careful separation and discrimination to avoid being misled by similitude and metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke contrasts wit and judgment: 'WIT lying most in the assemblage of ideas... JUDGMENT, on the contrary, lies quite on the other side, in separating carefully...'. He observes that quickness of wit does not guarantee clearness of judgment and that metaphors/allusions appeal to fancy rather than reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and determinacy prevent confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Having clear, determinate ideas prevents mistakes or confusions even if the same object sometimes produces different sensory impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke gives examples (taste in fever producing bitter from sugar) to show that distinct ideas remain distinct in the mind provided they are clear and determinate; clearness of idea counteracts sensory variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing / Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of comparing ideas (in extent, degree, time, place, etc.) produces the wide class of ideas called relations and is an essential cognitive operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'The COMPARING them one with another... is another operation of the mind about its ideas, and is that upon which depends all that large tribe of ideas comprehended under RELATION.' He notes limited degree of this faculty in animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounding / Composition of ideas (formation of complex ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can voluntarily put together simple ideas into complex ideas; these complex ideas fall under modes, substances, or relations and may be simple modes (variations of one simple idea) or mixed modes (combinations of different simple ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'Ideas thus made up of several simple ones put together, I call COMPLEX; ... I think they may be all reduced under these three heads:—1. MODES. 2. SUBSTANCES. 3. RELATIONS.' Examples: beauty (mixed mode), a dozen (simple mode). He emphasizes this compositional power is confined to the simple ideas provided by sensation and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and Abstraction (formation of general ideas / universals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words serve as outward signs of internal ideas; abstraction is the mental operation by which particular ideas are stripped of time/place/circumstance to become general ideas, enabling general names and universals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that without abstraction names would be endless; the mind makes particular ideas general by considering their 'precise, naked appearances' apart from concomitants. Example: whiteness abstracted from chalk, snow, or milk and named 'whiteness'. He asserts that this faculty distinguishes humans from brutes, who do not abstract or use general signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative cognitive capacities: brutes, idiots, and madmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke identifies degrees and kinds of cognitive capacity across creatures and human conditions: animals have perception and some retention but lack full powers of comparison, composition, and abstraction; idiots and madmen show different defects—idiots through lack of quickness/activity, madmen through disorderly combination of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's positions: birds learn tunes and retain patterns (memory), but brutes 'abstract not' and 'compare but imperfectly'; he argues animals likely lack general ideas and universal signs. On human pathologies: idiots lack quickness and invention, madmen have reason but from false premises—'madmen put wrong ideas together, and so make wrong propositions, but argue and reason right from them; idiots make very few or no propositions, and reason scarce at all.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and appeal to experience (epistemic procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke's methodological criterion: examine things as they are via experience and observation to discover the origins and operations of ideas; do not rely on supposed innate ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke repeatedly appeals to observation and experience as the 'only way' he can discover how ideas are brought into understanding: 'the best way to come to truth being to examine things as really they are...' He frames his account of faculties and ideas as conjecture to be checked by observation.
